overview: Imagine trying to find a kingdom that appears on a map for four centuries but steps into surviving history for only twelve years. Yueban is that puzzle. A later Chinese history traced its people to Northern Xiongnu followers left north of Kucha after a defeat around 89 CE, yet modern source study securely sees the name only from 437 to 448. In 437 envoys reached Northern Wei. In 448 they asked that empire to squeeze their Rouran enemies from the east while Yueban pressed from the west. The chronicle also preserves shiny buttered hair, frequent washing, sulfur used as medicine, weather-making claims and drum-and-dance rhythms adopted at the Wei court. These wonderful details still come through an outsider’s pen. Then Yueban disappears from dated records; theories linking it to Avars or Hephthalites disagree. The atlas makes the mystery bigger: one tiny unchanged polygon sits west of Lake Balkhash at 100, 200, 300 and 400, far from many historical placements around Ili, Chu, Tarbagatai or north of Issyk-Kul. Read it as a display shape, not a four-hundred-year border certificate.

periods.title: An atlas beginning, not a securely attested kingdom
periods.summary: The map starts Yueban at 100, echoing a later origin story after Northern Xiongnu defeats; no contemporary record securely names a Yueban state in this century.

periods.title: A long documentary silence
periods.summary: Northern Xiongnu groups had scattered, but the sources do not let us follow one continuous Yueban government through these generations or equate it with Southern Xiongnu communities in China.

periods.title: New Hunnic labels, uncertain continuities
periods.summary: Hunnic names appeared across Central Asia, yet the documentary gap after the Northern Xiongnu does not turn every similarly named group into one migrating people or prove a Yueban succession.

periods.title: Rouran expansion reshaped the western steppe
periods.summary: Shelun founded the Rouran imperial confederation in 402 and its influence reached the Ili and Tarim regions, forming the political setting in which Yueban first becomes visible.

periods.title: The brief, securely documented Yueban window
periods.summary: Yueban joined western embassies in 437 and in 448 used tribute and diplomacy to request Northern Wei military help against repeated Rouran pressure.

periods.title: Alliance action, then the record fades
periods.summary: Northern Wei mobilized after the 448 request, while Rouran entered a wider mid-fifth-century crisis; no clear Yueban victory or later dated Yueban notice is securely recorded.

periods.title: An atlas afterlife amid different fifth-century powers
periods.summary: The atlas keeps Yueban through 500, while Kidarite and Hephthalite rulers operated farther south with distinct coinages and chronologies; a direct Yueban transformation is unproved.

sections.title: Start with the exact atlas feature and its giant warning label

items.text: The exact id is yueban, labelled “Yueban” and indexed circa 100 to 500. Initial coverage calls it an approximate state with no card and four intervals: 100 to 200, 200 to 300, 300 to 400 and 400 to 500. Those intervals describe imported map files, not four centuries of documented government.

At 100 the target is one Polygon with one ring and nine coordinate positions. Its bounds are [71.41931419314193, 44.50546215401255, 75.33615336153363, 47.772249836919286], its raw coordinate SHA-256 is d5fce106a2f8d45ea140352a79c7db162273d47b573c146e5d47906126447ad2, and its canonical geometry hash is c3bbdc5b2d998c0a00c5c47d341e5155b01198a4ba1cf343b45ac0161fe8f6bc. Every count comes from decoded TopoJSON coordinates, not a screenshot.

Point tests place only the western Lake Balkhash test point inside. Tacheng, the Emil valley, Tarbagatai, Bortala, the Dzungarian Gate, Ili/Yining, Issyk-Kul, Suyab, eastern Balkhash, Altai, Urumqi, Turfan, Kucha, Kashgar, Tashkent, Fergana, Otrar and Dunhuang all fall outside. The result is geometric, not historical.

The 100, 200 and 300 snapshots have exactly the same raw coordinate hash. The 400 raw hash changes to b1d3e85fa37e2661e1bba78461e366f7b4aa5d1709acc90cbfe8e56357fc1766 only because the closed ring starts at another vertex; rotation- and direction-independent canonical hashes prove all four outlines are geometrically identical.

The exact target is absent at 1 BCE, 500 and 600. The index separately names earlier Xiongnu, Southern Xiongnu and later ruanruan; it contains no actual Xianbei, Kidarite or Hephthalite id. Map labels are separate data identities, and none should be silently merged into Yueban.

sections.title: The chronology is a twelve-year window inside a four-century polygon

items.text: The Wei Shu origin story looks back to Dou Xian’s defeat of the Northern Xiongnu in 89 CE and says weaker followers stayed north of Kucha. Because the history was compiled centuries later, this is retrospective ancestry, not a contemporary certificate that a Yueban state began in 100.

A modern multilingual sourcebook says Yueban appears in Chinese history only in 437 to 448. That narrow statement matters: earlier residents, ancestors or archaeological cultures may have existed, but the name and polity cannot be followed securely through the atlas years 100, 200 or 300.

In 437 Yueban was among western states whose envoys reached Northern Wei. The annal record does not supply the envoys’ names, route or conversations. Even the first appearance therefore cannot become a cinematic scene we pretend to reconstruct for readers today.

The last securely dated notice is 448: Yueban envoys came twice, requested a coordinated attack on Rouran from east and west, and offered court marvel stories. “After this they often sent tribute” may be a conventional closing formula; it supplies no list of later years, rulers or places.

Older UNESCO synthesis associates a Yueban realm near Balkhash with Northern Xiongnu migration and treats its roots as early. That is a historiographical reconstruction, not equal evidence to dated embassies. This card keeps the origin possibility while refusing to manufacture annual events from 100 to 436.

sections.title: Historical geography points east of the atlas shape

items.text: Wei Shu calls Yueban northwest of Wusun and gives a court-distance figure from the Northern Wei capital. Such directional geography is approximate and depends on what “Wusun” meant to the compiler; it does not plot a survey line or justify a modern national boundary.

Yu reconstructs a move from north of Kucha into former Wusun land in the Ili and Chu river valleys after Rouran pressure pushed Wusun toward the Pamirs. He repeatedly marks parts of this reconstruction as probable or possible, so the route belongs on a dotted line.

Selbitschka locates the small Yueban polity north of Issyk-Kul in modern northeastern Kyrgyzstan. That differs in detail from Ili and Chu valley or Tarbagatai placements, but all lie well east or southeast of the atlas polygon west of Lake Balkhash. Sources agree only approximately.

Rouran was a separate imperial confederation founded in 402. Kradin reconstructs its western reach to the Ili River and Tarim depression, with a core, dependent groups and military hierarchy. The 400 atlas likewise draws a huge ruanruan polygon distinct from tiny Yueban.

At 400 the separate Ruanruan feature contains Tacheng, Emil, Tarbagatai, Bortala, the Dzungarian Gate, Ili, eastern Balkhash, Altai, Urumqi and Turfan, while Yueban contains only western Balkhash. The imported display therefore reverses much of the historical placement and deserves an explicit geography warning.

sections.title: A ruler, envoys and a clever alliance come into view

items.text: Wei Shu reports more than 200,000 people over several thousand li and says Liangzhou people called the ruler “Chanyu King.” These are outsider estimates and remembered titles, not census sheets or proof of an unbroken imperial office. They do show a ranked leadership recognizable to Chinese informants.

Northern Wei “tribute” was active diplomacy rather than automatic surrender. Selbitschka shows that foreign courts used gifts and embassies to negotiate peace and help. Yueban’s 448 offering strengthened a practical request: pressure Rouran from two directions before more raids arrived.

The 437 embassy placed Yueban in a broad Western Regions network reaching the Northern Wei court. We do not know the envoys’ names, exact route, cargo or spoken language. Their arrival still demonstrates organized messengers, elite authorization and knowledge of a distant political opportunity.

In 448 Yueban asked Northern Wei to attack Rouran from the east while Yueban acted from the west. The emperor accepted, ordered forces ready and appointed a vanguard. This is the clearest Yueban political achievement: using distance, timing and a stronger partner as strategic tools.

Northern Wei forces drilled, toured north and stored supplies, but did not meet the Rouran force in the recorded expedition. Yu concludes that the court acted “to some extent” in cooperation, while the joint action lacked the expected effect. Alliance paperwork was real; victory remains unproved.

sections.title: Rouran conflict is vivid, but the chronicle likes a good story

items.text: Shelun created the Rouran imperial confederation in 402, organized forces by hundreds and thousands and expanded toward Ili and the Tarim. Kradin also identifies a grave Rouran crisis from 438 to 470. Yueban diplomacy belongs inside this larger contest, not in an empty steppe.

Wei Shu says Yueban first allied with Rouran, then a Yueban king visited with thousands, mocked Rouran washing customs and fled before pursuers caught him. Treat this as hostile court ethnography and a moralizing origin tale for war, not a hidden camera recording everyone’s cleanliness.

The same passage says Yueban ritual specialists summoned rain, wind, snow and flood against raiders. It proves that envoys reported supernatural protection and that a Chinese textual tradition preserved the claim. It does not prove weather control; storms remain weather, even when diplomats give them excellent publicity.

No reviewed source securely inventories a Yueban bow, saddle, armor or army size. Mounted warfare is plausible in the political setting, but borrowing every Xiongnu or Rouran weapon would erase differences. The safe military picture is raids, pursuit, envoys and planned pincer action: nothing more precise.

After 448, scholars have variously connected Yueban with European Avars or Hephthalites, while others reject those routes. Kidarites ruled Tokharistan and Gandhara and Hephthalites built a different later power. Similar “Hun” labels are clues for research, not permission to fuse dynasties.

sections.title: Herding, craft and exchange are regional clues, not a Yueban inventory

items.text: Modern archaeology rejects the cartoon in which every Central Asian “nomad” ate only meat and moved constantly. Eastern Kazakhstan and western Xinjiang show mixed herding, farming and craft production with varied mobility. Yueban may have shared that landscape, but no excavated economy bears its name tag.

Begash in eastern Kazakhstan has a Phase 4 dated about 70 to 550, conventionally called Wusun. It shows intermittent use by smaller groups, with hearths and trash pits rather than a permanent Yueban capital. The overlap in time and region makes comparison useful; attribution remains explicitly non-Yueban.

Phase 4 finds at Begash include broken or unfinished spindle whorls, an iron rivet, ceramic slag and a cut bronze plate. They reveal spinning, repair and small-scale production in a regional pastoral setting. They cannot identify Yueban women, workshops or uniforms without inscriptions or stronger context.

Dental calculus and isotope research in the eastern Dzhungar Mountains finds long traditions of ruminant dairy, horse products and millet, with more agrarian food after the era of Han and Xiongnu rivalry. That makes a mixed menu possible around Yueban’s world, but it is regional evidence, not their dinner receipt.

Yueban envoys also carried knowledge: the Northern Wei court ordered Yueban drum-and-dance rhythms placed in its Music Bureau. That is a real cultural transfer and a rare achievement visible in the text. We have the adoption notice, not the melody, choreography or surviving Yueban instrument.

sections.title: Families, ranks and learning mostly hide behind court politics

items.text: The surviving record distinguishes a king, accompanying followers, envoys, reported specialists and a large unnamed population. It does not explain councils, clans, taxes, property or succession. “Chanyu King” indicates remembered prestige, while actual power probably depended on followers and alliances we cannot enumerate.

No secure Yueban source gives household size, marriage rules, inheritance, pregnancy care or women’s named roles. Regional pastoral economies required extensive household labor, but assigning every task by gender would be modern guesswork. Women and families mattered; the archive simply does not describe them fairly.

No Yueban school, primer, teacher or child’s exercise survives. Children may have learned herding, spinning, routes and diplomacy by joining household work, yet that is an inference from regional activities. The honest lesson plan has many blank spaces and no made-up “typical school day.”

The embassy stories imply specialist learning: messengers navigated distant courts, performers knew music and dance, ritual experts knew ceremonies, and healers claimed plant knowledge. Sources never tell us who trained them, at what age or whether skills stayed inside families, so apprenticeship remains possible rather than proven.

A reported population above 200,000 is too round and too distant to treat as a modern census. It may signal that Northern Wei writers imagined a substantial polity. It cannot calculate family count, childhood survival, social percentages or the number of people living inside the atlas polygon.

sections.title: Hair could shine; houses, meals and play are harder to see

items.text: Regional comparison at Begash suggests repeatedly used winter camps near pasture rather than aimless wandering. During the Yueban-era phase, earlier houses were mostly out of use and smaller periodic occupations left hearths and refuse pits. No structure there is securely a Yueban family home.

Wei Shu says people cut hair level with the eyebrows and rubbed it with clarified butter until it shone. That unforgettable detail may preserve real grooming, but it comes through an outsider’s ethnographic contrast. It is not proof that every age, gender and season followed one hairstyle.

Clarified butter appears in the hair report, not on a Yueban menu. Regional science makes dairy, meat and millet plausible foods, while mixed-economy archaeology allows grain and plant products too. Exact dishes, cooking pots, feast rules and children’s portions remain unknown; shiny hair is not a cookbook.

Hearths, spindle whorls, iron pieces and trash pits show cooking, textile work, repair and waste disposal in the wider region. Yueban musicians supplied drum-and-dance patterns admired at court. Together they suggest busy work and performance, while no securely Yueban toy or game rule has been found.

The sources record embassies but no Yueban market list, coin series or caravan tariff. People and gifts moved far, so elite exchange clearly occurred. Ordinary barter, animal sales and craft circulation remain possibilities; the evidence cannot price even one sheep for us.

sections.title: Medicine, water, bathing and toilets need separate answers

items.text: Wei Shu describes a southern “Fire Mountain,” melted-looking rock and material people collected as medicine, identifying it as stone sulfur. The observation may join volcanic geography with mineral use, but the location is uncertain and the text gives no recipe, dose, illness or test of benefit.

A 448 embassy brought a performer or healer who claimed to stop terrible bleeding with herbs after cutting throats or crushing heads. The emperor reportedly tested the method on condemned prisoners. This is a sensational court marvel story and an ethical horror, not clinical proof or safe medical advice.

Weather-makers, sulfur collectors and herb specialists show that the chronicle associated Yueban with practical and ritual knowledge. It does not preserve diagnosis, childbirth care, wound cleaning or common remedies. Families certainly faced sickness and injury, but everyday medicine remains mostly outside the written spotlight.

Begash stood beside a spring-fed stream that still carries water year-round, illustrating why seasonal camps favored dependable water. Yueban reconstructions also cluster around major valleys. Neither fact proves pipes, wells or household storage, and the atlas polygon’s western-Balkhash position cannot answer a plumbing question.

The famous line says they bathed and rinsed three times daily before eating. It may express admired cleanliness through an outsider’s moral comparison. Bathing and mouth-rinsing are not toilet systems: no secure Yueban latrine, sewer, drain or waste rule has been identified, while regional trash pits are not privies.

sections.title: The surviving sentence is Chinese testimony about Yueban

items.text: The Book of Wei was compiled by Wei Shou and presented in 554, more than a century after the 448 embassy. Its Western Regions chapter preserves earlier reports but speaks in an outside court’s Classical Chinese voice. Genre, distance and later compilation all matter when reading daily-life claims.

Authentic written sample transmitted for the Yueban notice: “日三澡漱，然後飲食。” These eight Classical Chinese characters belong to an external Chinese textual tradition about Yueban. They are directly relevant evidence, but they are not an indigenous Yueban inscription, manuscript, alphabet, authorial voice or community self-description.

Modern Mandarin pinyin: “Rì sān zǎo shù, ránhòu yǐnshí.” Translation: “Three times a day they bathed and rinsed; only afterward did they eat and drink.” The pinyin helps present readers pronounce today’s Chinese reading; it is not a reconstruction of sixth-century pronunciation or Yueban speech.

Wei Shu says Yueban customs and language resembled Gaoche, but no securely Yueban-authored text survives and scholars disagree about early Hunnic languages. Names and outsider comparisons cannot invent a vernacular script. The sample must remain labelled external Classical Chinese court testimony.

The weather story shows reported ritual specialists, yet no named Yueban deity, temple or shared creed survives. After 448 the political name fades; people, families and practices may have joined later groups, but Avar, Kidarite, Hephthalite or other continuities remain hypotheses rather than a documented royal succession.

ending.text: Yueban has no documented final battle or extinction. The last secure dated action is the 448 alliance request; the atlas continues the unchanged polygon to its 500 seam, where the feature disappears. Later scholars proposed movement toward Europe, an Avar connection or identification with Hephthalites, but interdisciplinary work finds the bridges uncertain, while Kidarite and Hephthalite dynasties have their own southern settings and evidence. This bundle therefore marks 448 as the last attested political record, not the day families or communities vanished.
